doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

chapter: Jazz today and the business of events
title: The role of jazz in society in 2024
summary: Poston discusses the blurring of jazz with other music and how jazz is celebrated at major institutions without people understanding it.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Eight bars of time. That’s what you want right there. I’m going to see if I can put this — I was going to save this for later but it seems to me in reading about jazz history and society that at different periods jazz has had a place in American society, if it was the jazz era and the music that went with it — of course the swing era, the avante garde period, civil rights, that jazz has had an impact on that part of society. You don’t have to necessarily agree with me but I wonder if you think jazz — what is the role of jazz in society in 2024?

Well yeah, that’s a great question. I think — I mean the thing to me right now, I mean I think it’s, what I’ve noticed over the last few years is this great desire to kind of blur the lines of jazz and other musics. I assume that’s for commercial purposes. I never really thought too much about it, but at the radio station I see it all the time with CDs that we get and things like that. So I think jazz is at a point, for the 2024 part of it, I think there’s a certain perception — it may not be the same by everyone in society but I think there’s a certain perception of jazz and what jazz is and what it represents. And I think it’s, you know we’re in an age where it’s celebrated at Kennedy Center and at the White House and at Lincoln Center and things like that, which you know prior to what the 1980s that

really didn’t happen too much. So as jazz has become thought of as — and all the key words and all the phrases everyone uses of America’s classical music and this and that, I think it’s made people aware to a certain degree that it’s an important American creation and important to our society and important to our culture. The sad thing is is I don’t think it has educated people any more so as to what it is or why, but I think that there’s a perception of it as being — and I think you could say that probably about decade by decade, that the perception has changed or altered or enhanced as we get to this point. But yeah, it’s tough ‘cause I know just from personal experience, at least for me, is that I think it’s more difficult now as it’s ever been to have successful events and to have successful projects related to the music that — to draw an audience. In other words, I think unless something is subsidized, having it subsidized by a paying public is as difficult now as it’s ever been, unless it’s a festival or an event that uses the term jazz very loosely but it’s more of a music festival that has performers on it that will draw a big crowd. And of course as we know we’ve seen more and more of that, and that’s what I said in the beginning, this blurring of the lines kind of, you know that jazz has touched so many kinds of music that it’s okay now for rock groups to headline jazz concerts, or for whatever the case may be. So I don’t know if that’s healthy or unhealthy but it’s just something that I have to deal with on a daily basis, because the tendency — I mean if you’re not really passionate about it, and if you’re not really, you know depending on what’s your reason for why you’re doing what you’re doing, it’s easy I think to take the easier road of festival headliner or concert headliner or something that will guarantee. Now people will argue that that’s okay. You know people will argue that that’s okay you know, if it takes a certain headliner to subsidize the event so that everybody sees and hears everything else then that’s okay. I mean I certainly think you could make a case where it’s okay but I think there’s times it’s not okay as well. So, and I think there’s times that it’s unnecessary. So I guess that’s, you know that’s kind of an issue today.
